title: Given an array of integers that may include negative numbers, find the maximum sum obtainable from any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it with Kadane's algorithm and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

s1_definition.profdef: The maximum subarray sum problem asks for the largest possible sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an integer array that may contain negatives. Kadane's algorithm solves it in a single linear pass by maintaining, at each position, the best sum of a subarray ending exactly there, which is either the current element alone or the current element added to the best sum ending at the previous position, whichever is larger, while tracking the global maximum of those local bests.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily profit and loss figures for a trading desk, some positive gains and some negative losses, and wants the most profitable continuous stretch of days. As he walks day by day he asks a simple question: is my running streak still helping me, or should I abandon it and start fresh from today? If the streak has gone negative it is dead weight, so he drops it and starts over, always remembering the best streak total he has ever seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each element, either extend the running sum or restart from this element, and keep the best running sum ever seen.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The maximum subarray sum problem asks for the largest possible sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an integer array that may contain negatives. Kadane's algorithm solves it in a single linear pass by maintaining, at each position, the best sum of a subarray ending exactly there, which is either the current element alone or the current element added to the best sum ending at the previous position, whichever is larger, while tracking the global maximum of those local bests.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily profit and loss figures for a trading desk, some positive gains and some negative losses, and wants the most profitable continuous stretch of days. As he walks day by day he asks a simple question: is my running streak still helping me, or should I abandon it and start fresh from today? If the streak has gone negative it is dead weight, so he drops it and starts over, always remembering the best streak total he has ever seen.

**One line to remember:** At each element, either extend the running sum or restart from this element, and keep the best running sum ever seen.

sections.s2_technical:
Kadane's algorithm rests on one elegant observation. The maximum subarray must end at some position, so if for every position we can compute the maximum sum of a subarray that ends exactly there, then the overall answer is simply the largest of those per-position values. This reduces a two-dimensional search over all start and end pairs into a single linear scan.

We maintain two variables. The first, call it `currentMax`, is the maximum sum of a subarray ending at the current index. The second, call it `globalMax`, is the best answer seen so far. For each element we update the current max with `currentMax = Math.max(nums[i], currentMax + nums[i])`. This captures the key decision: either the best subarray ending here is the element by itself, which happens when the previous running sum was negative and therefore harmful, or it is the previous running sum extended by this element. After updating the current max we update the global max with `globalMax = Math.max(globalMax, currentMax)`.

The initialization matters and is a common source of bugs. Because the subarray must be non-empty and the array may be all negatives, we must start both variables at the first element, `currentMax = globalMax = nums[0]`, and then iterate from the second element. Starting the global max at zero would wrongly report zero for an all-negative array, when the correct answer is the single least-negative element. The senior-level nuance is exactly this: Kadane's correct handling of the all-negative case hinges on seeding from the first element rather than from zero.

If we also want the indices of the best subarray, we track a tentative start that resets whenever we choose to restart, and we commit the best start and end whenever the global max improves. The time complexity is linear, O(n), a single pass, and the space complexity is O(1), just a couple of scalars. Kadane's algorithm is the archetypal dynamic-programming-on-a-sequence technique and the baseline every interviewer expects for this problem.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a proprietary trading desk records daily profit and loss as a sequence of signed amounts, positive on winning days and negative on losing days. Risk management wants to identify the single most profitable continuous run of trading days, both its total and its start and end, because that run is used in performance attribution and in deciding which strategy periods to study. This is exactly the maximum subarray sum problem, with the twist that losing days are negative and a long run can be dragged down by them.

Problem 2 — Checking every possible run of days by brute force is quadratic and does not scale across the many desks and long histories the bank tracks. Kadane's algorithm gives a single linear pass per desk, and because it also yields the start and end indices, it directly produces the reportable date range, which is what makes the nightly performance report feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `ProfitStreakAnalyzer` service with a `bestProfitStreak` method implementing Kadane's algorithm and returning the total plus the start and end indices, and a runnable `MaxSubarrayDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's profit-and-loss sequences, logging restarts at fine level and the best streak at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's profit-and-loss sequence is -20, 50, -10, 40, -5, 30, -100, 10. We seed the current max and global max both at the first element, -20, with the tentative start, best start, and best end all at 0.

Step 1 at index 1, value 50: the current max -20 is negative, so we restart; current max becomes 50, tentative start becomes 1. Current max 50 beats global max -20, so global max becomes 50, best start 1, best end 1.

Step 2 at index 2, value -10: current max 50 is not negative, so we extend; current max becomes 40. Global max stays 50 because 40 is smaller.

Step 3 at index 3, value 40: current max 40 is not negative, extend; current max becomes 80. 80 beats 50, global max becomes 80, best start 1, best end 3.

Step 4 at index 4, value -5: extend; current max becomes 75. Global max stays 80.

Step 5 at index 5, value 30: extend; current max becomes 105. 105 beats 80, global max becomes 105, best start 1, best end 5.

Step 6 at index 6, value -100: current max 105 is not negative, extend; current max becomes 5. Global max stays 105.

Step 7 at index 7, value 10: current max 5 is not negative, extend; current max becomes 15. Global max stays 105.

The best profit streak is 105, spanning days 1 through 5, which is the run 50, -10, 40, -5, 30.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum subarray sum problem asks for the largest sum of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an array that may contain negatives, and I solve it with Kadane's algorithm in a single linear pass. The insight is that the best subarray must end somewhere, so if I compute, for every position, the best sum of a subarray ending exactly there, the overall answer is just the largest of those values. I keep a running current maximum and a global maximum, and at each element I decide whether to extend the running sum by this element or to restart from this element alone, choosing whichever is larger, then I update the global maximum.

The detail I always stress is initialization. Because the subarray must be non-empty and the array could be entirely negative, I seed both the current and global maximum from the first element and iterate from the second. If I lazily started the global maximum at zero, I would wrongly return zero for an all-negative array when the correct answer is the single least-negative element. That seeding is the quiet correctness hinge of Kadane's algorithm, and it is where most buggy implementations fail.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on a proprietary trading desk. Daily profit and loss arrived as a sequence of signed amounts, and risk management needed the single most profitable continuous run of days, both its total and its date range, for performance attribution. I extended the basic algorithm to track a tentative start that resets on each restart and to commit the best start and end whenever the global maximum improved, so the output was directly the reportable date range. The linear pass scaled easily across many desks and long histories in the nightly report.

The senior-level point I make is that Kadane's algorithm is the canonical example of dynamic programming collapsed onto a single sequence with constant memory, because the state I carry is just the best sum ending at the previous position. I also mention that recovering the indices requires the small bookkeeping of a tentative start, which many candidates omit, and that for monetary data in production I accumulate in a long or BigDecimal to avoid overflow. Explaining the extension to indices and the overflow safeguard on top of the core recurrence is what shows an interviewer I have used this beyond a textbook.
